entities.name: Al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya (The Islamic Group), founded in Egypt in the 1970s from the Islamic student movement at Egyptian universities — particularly Asyut University in Upper Egypt — became one of the most violent Islamist organizations in Egyptian history during the 1990s, responsible for assassinations, attacks on tourists, and the 1997 Luxor Massacre (killing 62 people, mostly foreign tourists, at the Temple of Hatshepsut) before renouncing violence in 1997-1999 and undergoing a theological transformation.

Al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya emerged from the same ideological milieu as Egyptian Islamic Jihad (which later merged with al-Qaeda): both were radicalized by the defeat of 1967, Sadat's peace with Israel, and the influence of Sayyid Qutb's prison writings arguing that contemporary Muslim-majority societies were in a state of jahiliyya (pre-Islamic ignorance) requiring revolutionary overthrow. The group was involved in the assassination of President Anwar Sadat in 1981 (in coalition with Islamic Jihad).

The organization's 1997 renunciation of violence — initiated by imprisoned leaders engaging in a theological review — was a significant moment in Islamist ideological evolution, eventually formalized in a 2002 document repudiating terrorist tactics on religious grounds. After the 2011 Egyptian Revolution, Al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya formed a political party (the Building and Development Party) and participated in parliamentary elections — completing an extraordinary transformation from designated terrorist organization to electoral participant in a single decade.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Al-Gama'a al-Islamiyya — responsible for Egypt's most deadly terrorist attack (Luxor 1997), involved in Sadat's assassination, but subsequently undergoing a landmark theological renunciation of violence and transforming into a political party — is one of the most significant case studies in Islamist radicalization and deradicalization.
